results.title: Rapid Point-of-care Testing to Inform Intrapartum Treatment of Group B Streptococcus–Colonized Women in Uganda - PMC
results.content: We evaluated the diagnostic performance of the HiberGene (HG) GBS loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) assay for the rapid detection of GBS in rectal/vaginal swabs collected from women in Uganda. In phase 1, 1294 rectal and vaginal swabs were collected from pregnant women and inoculated in enrichment (Lim) broth, which was then tested using the HG GBS LAMP assay (*sip* gene target) and culture on chromogenic agar. The results of this study demonstrate high sensitivity and specificity of the HG GBS LAMP assay for the detection of GBS rectovaginal colonization in our setting. If rapid, accurate, and affordable point of care of testing for GBS colonization could be developed to optimize the administration of IAP, this would minimize GBS transmission risk and greatly improve the disease burden in LMICs. In light of this, we evaluated the diagnostic performance of the HiberGene (HG) GBS loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) assay for the detection of maternal GBS rectovaginal colonization, comparing it to enrichment culture using the World Health Organization criteria for diagnostic test suitability [11]. This was a prospective diagnostic accuracy study evaluating HG's LAMP assay (index test) (HiberGene Diagnostics, Dublin, Ireland) by comparing its diagnostic performance against enrichment culture (reference test), the current gold standard method of detection [2]. There were 45 GBS-positive results detected by enrichment culture and 68 GBS-positive samples detected using the HG GBS LAMP assay (34 rectal swabs and 34 vaginal swabs) (Table 2). HG GBS LAMP Assay Evaluation Using Direct Swab Samples Compared Against Enrichment Culture (n = 166). This is the first study to investigate rapid diagnostic tests in labor for the assessment of GBS rectovaginal colonization in Uganda and the first to indicate acceptable sensitivity and specificity of the HG GBS LAMP assay, compared to culture, regardless of a pre-enrichment step. For direct swab testing, similar sensitivity results were reported in a prior study evaluating diagnostic accuracy the HG GBS LAMP assay in Ireland (92.2%) [14], as well as other studies evaluating rapid molecular-based assays, including the GeneOhm IDI-strep B (91.1%) [17] and quantitative PCR (95.5%) [18].

results.title: Influenza Rapid Diagnostic Tests - Medical Clinical Policy Bulletins | Aetna
results.content:
Title: Influenza Rapid Diagnostic Tests - Medical Clinical Policy Bulletins | Aetna
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidelines state that, despite the availability of rapid diagnostic tests, collecting clinical specimens for viral culture is critical, because only culture isolates can provide specific information regarding circulating strains and subtypes of influenza viruses. Investigators compared the sensitivity of a commercially available antigen-based rapid test (BinaxNOW Influenza A & B Rapid Test) with that of a real-time RT-PCR (rRT-PCR) assay specific for the hemagglutinin gene of the 2009 H1N1 virus. Staff members from Greenwich Hospital and the CT Department of Public Health collected data on symptoms for 63 patients and submitted naso-pharyngeal washings for testing using a rapid influenza diagnostic test (RIDT) for influenza A and B and rRT-PCR assay, thus affording an opportunity to assess the field performance of the RIDT. Cruz and associates (2010) evaluated the performance of a RIDT in detecting H1N1 2009 influenza A virus in respiratory samples from pediatric patients in comparison to that of rRT-PCR and viral culture. Of the 109 enrolled patients, the sensitivity, specificity, positive, and negative predictive values (PPV and NPV) of the Sofia FIA to detect influenza A virus were 82 %, 89 %, 77 %, and 89 %, respectively. Moreover, these researchers also encouraged similar studies to include relevant clinical perspectives to examine the diagnostic performance of any rapid influenza antigen tests, including the Sofia FIA. The authors concluded found that pooled sensitivities of the Quidel Sofia rapid influenza FIA were slightly below the target level (greater than or equal to 80 %) set by the FDA for both influenza A and B; thus, physicians should consider the possibility of false-negative results by this test, especially for adults. Rapid antigen-based diagnostic tests for influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), human metapneumovirus, and Streptococcus pneumoniae had sub-optimal sensitivity (range of 49 % to 84 %) but high specificity (greater than 80 %). ### Comparative Evaluation of Three Rapid Influenza Diagnostic Tests for Detection of Influenza A and B Viruses Using RT-PCR as Reference Method. Respiratory specimens were collected and tested for influenza A and B viruses using 3 RIDTs. The results were compared with those obtained using an RT-PCR assay from Shanghai Berger Medical Technology Co. Ltd.
